summary: Explains that the RFC Editor snapshots of Internet Official Protocol Standards, the xx00 documents, are replaced by a web page. Unpublished xx00 numbers up to 7000 are never issued, and from RFC 7100 they can be assigned.

eli5.summary: Round numbers were saved for a list that is now online, so they are free for use.

questions: official protocol standards list web page
subtitle: RFC numbering for protocol standards documents goes online

tldr.problem: For decades, RFC numbers ending in 00 were reserved for snapshots of the Internet Official Protocol Standards, but online lists now serve this purpose better.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC Editor moved the standards list to a web page that updates automatically, eliminating the need for periodic RFC snapshots.
tldr.outcome: RFC numbers ending in 00 through 7000 are marked never issued, and from RFC 7100 onward they are available for normal use.

today: RFC 7101 is an Informational document that documents this administrative change. The official list of Internet standards is now maintained as a live web page at the RFC Editor site.

sections.title: The Tradition of xx00 Documents
sections.content: Since RFC 1083 in 1988, the RFC Editor periodically published snapshots of the Internet Official Protocol Standards as documents with numbers ending in 00, such as RFC 1000, 1100, 1200. RFC 5000, published in May 2008, was the last such snapshot. These documents served a critical purpose before the internet: they let people know which protocols were official standards.
sections.eli5: For a long time, every hundredth RFC was a list of all the important protocols.

sections.title: Moving to the Web
sections.content: In 2000, the RFC Editor created an online list of protocol standards that updates automatically. After more than a decade with this web page available, and consensus from the IETF that the periodic snapshots are no longer needed, the official standards information is now provided only online. The tradition of publishing these snapshots ends.
sections.eli5: A website can show live information better than old paper, so printed lists are no longer needed.

sections.title: Cleanup of RFC Numbers
sections.content: All RFC numbers ending in 00 through RFC 7000 are now marked by the RFC Editor as never issued. Starting with RFC 7100, numbers ending in 00 are available for regular use. STD 1, the subseries identifier for the standards list, is moved to Historic status. This frees up numbering space and clarifies the state of the record.
sections.eli5: The RFC Editor took those round numbers off the shelf and made them available for new documents to use.

references.text: Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency and Internet Activities Board, "IAB official protocol standards", RFC 1083, December 1988.
RFC Editor, "Internet Official Protocol Standards", STD 1, RFC 5000, May 2008.
Resnick, P., "Retirement of the 'Internet Official Protocol Standards' Summary Document", BCP 9, RFC 7100, December 2013.
